en: The Larger Prajñāpāramitā (LPG 1r): Siddham. Homage to the Omniscient One! Thus have I heard: at one time the Blessed One was dwelling at Rājagṛha on the Vulture Peak Mountain together with a great community of monks, about five thousand monks in number.
By all those Arhats— whose taints were exhausted, who were free from afflictions, who had attained mastery, whose minds were well-liberated, whose wisdom was well-liberated,
who were noble steeds, great elephants, who had accomplished what was to be done, performed their duties, laid down the burden, achieved their own goal,
completely destroyed the fetters of existence, whose minds were well-liberated through right knowledge, and who had reached the supreme perfection of mastery over all mental states.

With the exception of one person— namely, the venerable Ānanda, who was still a learner (śaikṣa) and a stream-enterer (srotāpanna)— together with about five hundred bhikṣuṇīs headed by Yaśodharā and Mahāprajāpatī, and with a great multitude of male and female lay followers (upāsaka and upāsikā),
all of whom had seen the Dharma, and together with a vast assembly of bodhisattvas, immeasurable and incalculable in number.

All of them were bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who had attained the dhāraṇīs and attained the samādhis; they dwelt in emptiness, whose range was the signless, whose vows were non-conceptual, and who had attained the patient acceptance of the equality of all phenomena; they were endowed with unimpeded vows, had penetrated the method of the analytical knowledges of inexhaustible exposition, sported with the great superknowledges, and possessed superknowledges that never declined.

They were men whose speech was worthy of being accepted; who were free from indolence and had initiated heroic vigor; who were indifferent to body and life; who were without guile and not talkative; whose minds were free from thoughts of kin or gain; who taught the Dharma without worldly motives; who had reached the ultimate limit of patience regarding the profound Dharma;
who had attained great fearlessness; whose minds were unshrinking; who had completely transcended all the works of Māra; and whose karmic obscurations were stilled.
They had vanquished the adversaries of karma and the afflictions; they were unsurpassed by any proponents of opposing doctrines;

they were difficult for all śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas to fathom; they were skilled in the analytical discernment and exposition of the Dharma; they had well-undertaken their vows throughout incalculable eons; they possessed smiling faces and were the first to speak; they were free from frowns and spoke with smooth and sweet words; and they were skilled in conversing with others through the singing of verses.
They possessed unassailable eloquence and the fearlessnesses that overwhelm infinite assemblies; they were skilled in the knowledge of how to emerge from the teachings of infinite millions of eons;

they were devoted to the Dharma as being like an illusion, a mirage, the moon reflected in water, a dream, an echo, an optical illusion, the sky, a city of the gandharvas, a reflection, and a magical creation;
their minds were free from despondency, and they were skilled in entering into the inclinations and the subtle knowledge of the mental movements of all sentient beings.

They possessed minds unimpeded toward all sentient beings and were endowed with supreme patience; they were skilled in the knowledge that penetrates the true nature of all phenomena, yet found the profound nature of reality difficult to fathom. They had attained mastery over their own minds and achieved all forms of sovereignty. Liberated from the obscurations of all karma, afflictions, and views, they were skilled in explaining dependent origination and had entered the inexhaustible method of the profound dependent origination. They were entirely free from all views, latent tendencies, and active outbursts of defilement.
They had abandoned all fetters, were skilled in the knowledge that penetrates the truths, and were constantly and perpetually devoted to the realization that all phenomena are like echoes.

They were proficient in teaching the immeasurable methods of the Dharma, skilled in leading others into the realization of suchness, and sustained by their vows and undertakings for the array of infinite Buddha-fields.
They were perpetually present in the samādhi of recollecting the Buddhas residing in incalculable world-systems, and were skilled in approaching all Buddhas whenever they appeared in the world.

They were skilled in exhorting immeasurable Buddhas; skilled in pacifying the afflictions of sentient beings through the arousal of various views; skilled in entering the knowledge that sports in the accomplishment of hundreds of thousands of samādhis;
and endowed with qualities and praises that would not be exhausted even throughout infinite eons—such as, for example, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Bhadrapāla.
And by Ratnākara,
and by Ratnagarbha,
and by Ratnadatta.
And by Susārthavāha,
and by Naladatta, and by Guhaputra.
And by Varuṇadeva and Indradeva,
and by Bhadrapāla,
and by Uttaramati.
And by Viśeṣamati, and by Vardhamānamati, and by Anantamati.
And with Amoghadarśin,
Anāvaraṇamati,
and Susaṃprasthita.
And by Suvikrāntavikrāmin,
Anantavīrya,
and Nityodyukta.
And by Nityaprayukta (Ever-Exerted), and by Anikṣiptadhura (One Who Does Not Cast Off the Burden),
and by Sūryagarbha (Sun-Womb).
and by the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Anupamamati,
and by Avalokiteśvara;
And by Mahāsthāmaprāpta,
and by Mañjuśrī Kumārabhūta,
and by Mārabalapramardin.
And by Vajramati,
and by Ratnamudrāhasta,
and by Nityotkṣiptahasta.
And Mahākaruṇācintin, and Mahāvyūha, and Vyūharāja.
And with Merukūṭa and the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Maitreya, and with these and many other hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of Bodhisattvas— then,
at that time, the Blessed One himself prepared a lion-throne and sat down cross-legged upon it.
Having folded his legs crosswise, set his body erect, and established mindfulness before him, he sat down there and entered the concentration called Samādhirāja,
in which all concentrations are included,
entered, subsumed, and brought together.
Then the Blessed One, mindful and clearly comprehending, arose from that concentration and surveyed this buddha-field with his divine eye.

Having surveyed it, he emitted light from his entire body; from beneath him, from the two thousand-spoked wheels on the soles of his feet, sixty times sixty hundred-thousand million-billion rays of light issued forth.
And from the ten toes of his feet, sixty-six hundred thousand *niyutas* of millions of rays of light issued forth.
Likewise, from both ankles, both shanks, both knees,

both thighs, from the waist, from the circle of the navel, from both sides, and from the *śrīvatsa*, the mark of a Great Man on his chest, sixty-six [hundred thousand *niyutas* of millions of rays] issued forth.
Hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of rays of light issued forth.
From each of the ten fingers of his hands, sixty-six hundred thousand million billion rays of light issued forth;
likewise from both arms, from both shoulders, and from the four [joints] of his neck.
From his forty teeth, from his two eyes, from his two ears,

from his two nostrils, from the *ūrṇā* hair between his eyebrows, from the *uṣṇīṣa* on top of his head, and from the opening of his mouth, sixty-six hundred thousand *koṭī-niyuta* rays of light issued forth.

And all those hundreds of thousands of myriads of koṭis of rays, having pervaded this entire great trichiliocosm with a great radiance, pervaded world-systems in the eastern direction as numerous as the sands of the river Ganges with that great radiance.

In this way, in the southern direction, the western, the northern, below, above, and indeed all around throughout the ten directions— in each individual direction— they pervaded world-systems as numerous as the sands of the river Gaṅgā with a great radiance.

And those beings by whom that radiance was seen, and those who were touched by that manifestation of light rays, they all became fixed in their destiny for unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening.

Then the Blessed One again emitted light from all his pores, by which light this great trichiliocosm world-system was suffused with a vast radiance; and in the eastern direction, world-systems as numerous as the sands of the river Gaṅgā were suffused with a vast radiance. Likewise in the southern direction, in the western, in the northern, and below.

Above, and indeed all around in the ten directions, world-systems as numerous as the sands of the river Gaṅgā in each single direction were pervaded by a great radiance. All those beings who saw that radiance and all those who were touched by that radiance became fixed in their destiny for unexcelled, perfect enlightenment.
Then the Blessed One again caused this great trichiliocosm world-system to be pervaded by a great radiance with that natural light of the Tathāgata;
he also caused world-systems in the eastern direction, as numerous as the sands of the river Ganges, to be pervaded by a great radiance.

In this way, in the southern direction, the western, the northern, below, above, and indeed all around in the ten directions, he pervaded world-systems as numerous as the sands of the river Ganges in each single direction with that great radiance. And those beings who saw that radiance and those who were touched by that radiance— all of them became fixed in their destiny for unexcelled, perfect enlightenment.

Then the Blessed One, having extended his tongue-faculty from the opening of his mouth, pervaded this entire trichiliocosm with that tongue-faculty and manifested a smile. From that tongue-faculty, there issued forth many hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of rays of light of various colors.
And upon every ray of light there stood lotuses made of various jewels, shining with the luster of gold, having a thousand petals;
they were variegated, beautiful to behold,
delightful, golden-hued, and fragrant.
They were soft, with a pleasant touch like that of kācalindika cloth.
And upon those lotuses, forms of the Tathāgatas were seated, teaching the Dharma— namely,
this very teaching of the Dharma connected with the six perfections— and they proceeded to world-systems in the eastern direction as numerous as the sands of the river Ganges.
Having gone there, they taught the Dharma— namely,
this very teaching of the Dharma associated with the six perfections. In the same way, in the southern direction,
the western, the northern, the nadir, the zenith, and indeed all around in the ten directions, in each single direction, [there were Buddhas] as numerous as the sands of the river Ganges.

They went to world-systems, and having gone there, they taught the Dharma; that is to say, this very teaching of the Dharma associated with the six perfections. And all those beings by whom that Dharma was heard became fixed in their destiny for unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.

Then the Blessed One, seated upon that very lion-throne, entered the Buddha-samādhi called "The Lion’s Play" and performed such a miraculous feat (*ṛddhyabhisaṃskāra*) that, by means of this performed miracle, this great trichiliocosm world-system shook, trembled, and quaked in six ways.
It quaked, it quaked violently, it quaked intensely; it shook, it shook violently, it shook intensely;

it trembled, it trembled violently, it trembled intensely; it roared, it roared violently, it roared intensely; it resounded, it resounded violently, it resounded intensely; it rose up at the edges and sank down in the middle.

The center rose up while the edges sank down; it became soft, smooth, subtle, and a producer of all happiness. Then, in that very instant, moment, and second, all the hells, animal births, the world of Yama, the unfavorable states, the states of woe, and the fallen conditions within this triple-thousand great-thousandfold world system [disappeared].
They were all completely eradicated, and all those beings were reborn into the commonality of human beings;
they were reborn into the commonality of the gods of the Four Great Kings, the Trāyastriṃśa, the Yāma, the Tuṣita, the Nirmāṇarati, and the Paranirmitavaśavartin gods. Then those humans...
And those gods, through that very joy, serene confidence, and gladness, recollected their former births.
Having recollected them, having attained joy, serene confidence, and gladness, they approached the Blessed One; having approached, with palms joined, they paid homage to the Blessed One.
In this same way, it occurred in world systems as numerous as the sands of the river Ganges in the eastern direction, and likewise in the southern, western, and northern directions.

Below, above, and all around— in each of the ten directions throughout world-systems as numerous as the sands of the river Gaṅgā— all hells, all animal births, and all realms of Yama were utterly destroyed, and all unfavorable conditions came to an end; and all those beings were reborn into the common lot of human beings.
Then those humans and those gods, through that very joy, serene faith, and gladness, recollected their former births.

Having recollected them, having attained joy, serene faith, and gladness, they approached the Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Perfectly Awakened Ones who were residing in their respective Buddha-fields; having approached them, they stood with palms joined in reverence.
They paid homage to those Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Perfectly Awakened Ones.
Then, at that very moment, all those beings in this triple-thousand great thousandfold world system who were blind from birth also saw forms with their eyes.
The deaf heard sounds with their ears;
the insane regained their mindfulness;
and those with distracted minds attained a state of non-distraction.
The naked obtained robes;
the poor obtained wealth;
those who were hungry obtained food.
The thirsty obtained drink;

those afflicted by disease became free from disease; those with impaired faculties had their faculties restored; those with exhausted bodies became free from exhaustion; and those who were not separated from unwholesome conduct of body, speech, and mind, and unwholesome livelihood, became free from such unwholesome conduct of body, speech, and mind, and unwholesome livelihood.

And all beings came to possess a mind of equanimity toward all beings—namely, a mind of equanimity like that toward a mother, father, brother, or sister; a mind of equanimity like that toward a friend, kinsman, or companion. All beings were endowed with the ten paths of wholesome action; they were celibate, pure, free from the stench of impurity, and devoid of all unwholesome thoughts. At that time, all beings were fully possessed of every happiness.
They were endowed with such happiness as that of a monk who has attained the third dhyāna; and at that time, all sentient beings were endowed with such wisdom that they knew:
"Excellent is giving! Excellent is self-control! Excellent is restraint! Excellent is truth!"
"Excellent is heedfulness; excellent is loving-kindness; excellent is compassion; excellent is non-violence toward living beings.

Then the Blessed One, seated upon that very lion-throne, [beheld] this great trichiliocosm world-system, including Mount Sumeru, the Cakravāḍa mountains, the abodes of the gods, along with Indra, Brahmā, Vaśavartin, and the Śuddhāvāsa heavens.
Having surpassed the entire host of gods and demons, he stands resplendent, shining, glowing, and radiant with light, complexion, majesty, and glory.

Just as a powerful sun shines in a perfectly clear sky, or like the orb of the moon on a full-moon night, even so the Blessed One, having surpassed world-systems as numerous as the sands of the river Ganges in the eastern direction, [surpasses them] in the southern direction.

In the west, in the north, below, above, and indeed throughout the ten directions, he stands having surpassed world-systems as numerous as the sands of the river Gaṅgā; he shines, glows, blazes, and radiates with splendor, color, brilliance, and majesty, just as, for example:
Sumeru, the king of mountains, stands surpassing all other mountains; it is beautiful, radiant, glowing, and resplendent.

Just as the lunar disk, standing surpassing all the forms of the stars, is beautiful, radiant, glowing, and brilliant; just as the solar disk, standing surpassing all other lights, is beautiful, radiant, glowing, and brilliant.

In the same way, the Blessed One, having surpassed the world with its gods, its Indras, its Māras, its Brahmās, and its Śuddhāvāsa deities in the ten directions, stands resplendent, shines, glows, and radiates with splendor,
complexion, majesty, and glory. Furthermore, he manifested here within this trichiliocosm a manifestation of his natural physical body exactly as it is.

Then, all the divine hosts in this triple-thousand great-thousand world system— from those of the Śuddhāvāsa realm down to the Brahmakāyika, Paranirmitavaśavartin, Nirmāṇarati, Tuṣita, Yāma, Trāyastriṃśa,
and Cāturmahārājakāyika gods— all beheld the Tathāgata seated upon the lion throne.

They were satisfied, elated, joyful, and filled with gladness and cheer; taking divine flowers, divine garlands, divine perfumes, divine ointments, divine powders, divine garments, and divine blue lotuses, red lotuses, white water lilies, white lotuses, nalinis, and saugandhikas.
Taking divine kesara flowers, tamāla leaves, divine robes,
divine ornaments,
divine parasols, divine banners, and divine flags, they approached the place where the Blessed One was.
Having approached, they scattered, showered, and strewn the Blessed One with those flowers and so forth, up to the parasols, banners, and flags.

And those humans in this great trichiliocosm world-system who were to be disciplined and had become fit vessels, having taken flowers growing in water and on land, approached the place where the Blessed One was and [honored] the Tathāgata.
They offered worship;
and all those flowers and so forth, up to the umbrellas, banners, and flags, were scattered over the Blessed One.
Immediately, through the Blessed One’s empowerment, [a canopy] equal in measure to the triple-thousand great-thousand world system appeared over the Blessed One.

In the sky above, at the junction of the peaks, a great peaked pavilion (kūṭāgāra) made of flowers and other materials was established. From that peaked pavilion, divine flower-garlands and silk streamers hung down, hung down, and hung down completely.
And by those flower-garlands and silk streamers, this great trichiliocosm world-system shone and gleamed exceedingly with the golden-colored radiance of the Blessed One’s majesty.
It blazed and shone forth;

and just as this trichiliocosm was so illuminated, even so were world-systems as numerous as the sands of the river Gaṅgā in the eastern direction illumined and pervaded, and likewise in the southern, western, and northern directions.
From below to above, as far as the world-systems in all ten directions were illuminated and made manifest.
There, when the people of Jambudvīpa saw the Tathāgata’s body, which was so beautiful as to never tire the sight, this thought occurred to them:
"The Tathāgata is seated right before us, teaching the Dharma."
Just as it was for the humans of Jambudvīpa, so it was for those of Godānīya, Pūrvavideha, and Uttarakuru;
and for the gods of the Four Great Kings’ realm up to the Aghanistha gods— it was thus for all sentient beings in the thousandfold world system,
the two-thousandfold world system, and the three-thousandfold great thousandfold world system— that this occurred before them.
"The Tathāgata is seated and teaching the Dharma.

Then the Blessed One, seated upon that very lion throne, again emitted a radiance, by which radiance this great trichiliocosm world-system was once more illuminated; by that illumination, [whatever was there]...

In this great trichiliocosm, all those beings saw the Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Perfectly Enlightened Ones, together with their assemblies of disciples, in world-systems in the eastern direction as numerous as the sands of the river Ganges;
and likewise, those beings who were in world-systems in the eastern direction as numerous as the sands of the river Ganges also saw this great trichiliocosm.
They beheld the world-system and the Blessed One, the Tathāgata Śākyamuni, accompanied by his retinue of the community of monks;

and just as it was in the eastern direction, so it was in the south, the west, the north, below, above, and indeed all around in the ten directions, in as many worlds as there are grains of sand in the river Gaṅgā.
The beings in those world-systems also saw this great trichiliocosm, as well as the Blessed One, the Tathāgata Śākyamuni, together with his retinue of the community of monks.

Then, having passed beyond world-systems as numerous as the sands of the river Gaṅgā in the eastern direction, there is a world-system at the very end called Ratnāvatī. There, a Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha named Ratnākara resides, stays, and maintains himself;
he thoroughly proclaims this very Perfection of Wisdom to the Bodhisattvas, the Mahāsattvas.
Then, in that world-system, a bodhisattva mahāsattva named Samantaraśmi, having seen that great radiance,

that great earthquake, and the body of the Tathāgata, approached where the Blessed One, the Tathāgata Ratnākara, was; having approached, he addressed the Blessed One, the Tathāgata Ratnākara, as follows:

He asked: "Blessed One, what is the cause, what is the condition for the appearance of this great radiance in the world, and for this great earthquake, and for such a body of the Tathāgata being seen?
When this was said, the Blessed One, the Tathāgata Ratnākara, [addressed] that Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Samantaraśmi.
He said this: "Noble son, in the western direction there is a world-system named Sahā; there the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha named Śākyamuni resides, stays, and maintains himself.
He thoroughly proclaims the perfection of wisdom to the Bodhisattvas, the Mahāsattvas."

Such was his majestic power. Then the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Samantaraśmi said this to the Blessed One, the Tathāgata Ratnākara: "Blessed One, I would go to that Sahā world-system in order to see, pay homage to, and attend upon the Blessed One Śākyamuni, the Tathāgata, Arhat, and Samyaksaṃbuddha."

And to those bodhisattva mahāsattvas, and to all those who had become youths, who had attained the dhāraṇīs and the analytical knowledges (pratisaṃvid), and who had attained mastery over meditative concentrations and attainments,
that Blessed One, the Tathāgata Ratnākara, said:
"Go, noble son, to behold this Tathāgata Śākyamuni, the Arhat, the Perfectly Awakened One, whenever you deem it the right time.
Then the Tathāgata Ratnākara gave a thousand golden-hued, thousand-petaled lotuses, together with their rays, to Samantaraśmi.

He gave them to the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva, saying: "Noble son, scatter these lotuses over that Blessed One Śākyamuni, the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha. And, noble son, you should be one who dwells with full awareness in that Buddha-field. Why is that? Because, noble son, those Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas are difficult to approach."
"Do not let those who have been born in that world-system suffer there.

Then the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Samantaraśmi, having taken from the presence of the Blessed One Ratnākara, the Tathāgata, Arhat, and Perfectly Enlightened One, those thousand-petaled lotuses with a golden luster, together with many others...
Together with hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of bodhisattvas— both householders and renunciants, and in the forms of boys and girls—

he vanished from that buddha-field and paid homage, veneration, respect, and worship to all the Buddhas, Blessed Ones, as many as were dwelling, visible, and maintaining themselves in the eastern direction, with flowers, garlands, perfumes, and ointments.

Accompanied by parasols, banners, and flags, with great bodhisattva honor and great bodhisattva majesty, he approached the place where the Blessed One Śākyamuni, the Tathāgata, Arhat, and Samyaksaṃbuddha was; having approached,
he bowed his head at the feet of the Blessed One Śākyamuni, the Tathāgata, Arhat, and Samyaksaṃbuddha, and stood to one side.
Standing to one side, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Samantaraśmi said this to the Blessed One:
"Blessed One, the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha Ratnākara inquires after the Blessed One’s freedom from affliction, freedom from illness, ease of movement, strength, and well-being."

And these thousand-petaled lotuses, radiant as gold, were sent by that Blessed One for the purpose of making an offering to the Blessed One. Then the Blessed One, having taken those lotuses, [proceeded] toward those worlds in the eastern direction, as numerous as the sands of the river Ganges.

He cast them toward the Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas in all the world-systems; then all those world-systems became filled with those lotuses, and upon those lotuses, forms of the Tathāgatas sat and taught the Dharma,
namely, beginning with these very six perfections.
And those beings who heard that teaching of the Dharma became fixed in their destiny for unexcelled, perfect enlightenment.
Those householders and renunciants, as well as boys and girls, honored, revered, respected, and worshiped the Tathāgata with their respective roots of merit.

In the same way, having passed beyond as many world-systems in the southern direction as there are grains of sand in the river Gaṅgā, there is a world-system at the very end named Sarvaśokāpagatā. There dwells, remains, and maintains his life the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha named Aśokaśrī.
There is a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva named Vigataśoka; [the description] should be carried out in detail as before.
In this way, in the western direction there is a world-system named Upaśāntā; there a Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha named Ratnārcis resides, stays, and maintains himself.
And there is a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva named Cāritramati—for all of which the detailed description should be supplied as before.
In the northern direction there is a world-system named Jayā; there a Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha named Jayendra resides, stays, and maintains his life.
There is a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva named Jayadatta—[the description] should be carried out in detail as before.

Likewise, in the northeastern direction, there is a world-system named Samādhyalaṃkṛtā; there dwells, remains, and maintains his life the Tathāgata named Samādhihastyuttaraśrī. Therein is a bodhisattva mahāsattva named Vijayavikrāmī, and so on, as should be described in detail.

In the southeastern direction, there is a world-system named Surucirā Bodhimaṇḍālaṃkāra; there dwells, remains, and maintains his life a Tathāgata named Padmottaraśrī. There, a bodhisattva mahāsattva named Padmahasta [resides], and so on, as should be described in detail.
In the southwestern direction, there is a world-system named Vigataraja-saṃcaya; there dwells, remains, and maintains his life a Tathāgata named Sūryamaṇḍalaprabhāsottamaśrī.
Therein is a bodhisattva mahāsattva named Sūryapratibhāsa, [and so on] as should be detailed at length.

In the northwestern direction there is a world-system named Vaśībhūtā; there dwells, remains, and maintains his life a Tathāgata named Ekacchatra. There, a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva named Ratnottama [resides], and so on, as should be described in detail.
(LPG 7r) In the downward direction is a world-system named Padmā; there dwells, remains, and maintains his life a Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha named Padmaśrī.

There is a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva named Padmottara—[the description] should be carried out in detail as before. Beyond world-systems in the upward direction as numerous as the sands of the river Gaṅgā, there is a world-system which is the very last, named Nandā. There...
The Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha named Nandaśrī resides, stays, and maintains himself there;
he thoroughly proclaims this very perfection of wisdom to the bodhisattva mahāsattvas.
Now, in that world-system, there was a bodhisattva mahāsattva named Nandadatta who [beheld] that great radiance.

Having seen that great earthquake and the physical form of the Tathāgata, he approached the Blessed One, the Tathāgata Nandaśrī; having approached, he said this to the Blessed One, the Tathāgata Nandaśrī:
"Blessed One, what is the cause, what is the reason for the appearance of this great radiance in the world?"
"And yet, amidst this great earthquake, such a body of the Tathāgata is visible.
When this was said, the Blessed One, the Tathāgata Nandaśrī, spoke thus to the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Nandadatta:
"Noble son, in the direction below there is a world-system named Sahā; therein dwells the one named Śākyamuni."
The Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, dwells, remains, and sustains himself;
he fully reveals the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*) to the bodhisattvas, the mahāsattvas.
Such is his majestic power. Then the bodhisattva mahāsattva Nandadatta [approached] that Blessed One, Nandaśrī.

He said this to the Tathāgata: "O Blessed One, I would go to that Sahā world-system in order to behold, pay homage to, and attend upon the Blessed One Śākyamuni, the Tathāgata, Arhat, and Samyaksaṃbuddha;
and [to see] those Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas and all those youths who have attained the dhāraṇīs and the analytical knowledges."
The Blessed One, the Tathāgata Nandaśrī, who has attained mastery over all meditative concentrations and attainments,
said: "Go, noble son, to behold that Tathāgata Śākyamuni, the Arhat, the Perfectly Awakened One, whenever you deem it the right time."

Then the Tathāgata Nandaśrī gave a thousand golden-hued, thousand-petaled lotuses to the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Nandadatta, saying: "Noble son, scatter these lotuses over that Blessed One, the Tathāgata Śākyamuni, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha; and, noble son, remain there mindful of your conduct."
It would be so in that buddha-field. Why is that? Because, noble son, those bodhisattva mahāsattvas who have been born in that world-system are difficult to approach;

do not let yourself be harmed there. Then the bodhisattva mahāsattva Nandadatta [received] those gold-colored [lotuses] from the presence of that Blessed One, the Tathāgata, Arhat, and Samyaksaṃbuddha Nandaśrī.
Taking thousand-petaled lotuses, together with many hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of bodhisattvas—

both householders and renunciants, and in the forms of boys and girls— he vanished from that buddha-field and paid homage, revered, honored, and respected all the Buddhas, Blessed Ones, as many as were residing, visible, and maintaining their lives in the direction above.
Honoring him with flowers, garlands, perfumes, ointments, and even with parasols, banners, and flags— with the great majesty of a bodhisattva and the great power of a bodhisattva—
he approached the Blessed One Śākyamuni, the Tathāgata, Arhat, and Samyaksaṃbuddha; having approached, he...

Having bowed his head at the feet of the Blessed One, Śākyamuni, the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Perfectly Awakened One, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Nandadatta stood to one side. Standing to one side, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Nandadatta addressed the Blessed One: "Blessed One, the Tathāgata, Arhat, and Perfectly Awakened One Nandaśrī inquires after the Blessed One’s freedom from illness and freedom from affliction."

Lightness of movement, strength, and a state of dwelling in pleasant contact— these were the thousand-petaled lotuses, radiant as gold, sent by that Blessed One for the purpose of honoring the Blessed One.
Then the Blessed One, having taken those lotuses, [proceeded] toward those worlds in the zenith, as numerous as the sands of the river Gaṅgā.

He cast them toward the Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas in all the world-systems; then, by those lotuses, all those world-systems were filled. And upon those lotuses, forms of the Tathāgatas sat and taught the Dharma, namely, beginning with these very six perfections.
And those beings who heard that teaching of the Dharma became fixed in their destiny for unexcelled, perfect enlightenment.
Those bodhisattvas as well— both householders and renunciants, boys and girls— honored, revered, respected, and worshiped the Tathāgata with their respective roots of merit.

Then, in that very instant, moment, and second, this great trichiliocosm became composed of jewels; it was strewn with various flowers, draped with silk streamers and garlands, perfumed by incense burners, and adorned with trees bearing every kind of flower and fragrance—
just like the world-system Padmāvatī belonging to the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha Samantakusuma.
The Buddha-field where Mañjuśrī Kumārabhūta dwells, as well as the divine son Susthitamati and other bodhisattvas, mahāsattvas of great majesty.
This is the first chapter, the Introduction, of the *Prajñāpāramitā*.
And when the Blessed One perceived that the world with its gods, its Māras, and its Brahmās, together with this generation of recluses and brahmins,
gods and humans, as well as those Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas— who for the most part were still youths— had all assembled, the Blessed One then addressed the venerable Śāradvatīputra:

"In this regard, Śāradvatīputra, a bodhisattva mahāsattva who wishes to fully awaken to all phenomena in all their aspects should apply himself to the perfection of wisdom. When this had been said, the venerable Śāriputra addressed the Blessed One as follows: "How, Blessed One, should a bodhisattva mahāsattva who wishes to fully awaken to all phenomena in all their aspects [apply himself]?"
"One should practice the yoga of the perfection of wisdom. When this was said, the Blessed One spoke thus to the venerable Śāradvatīputra:

"In this regard, Śāradvatīputra, a bodhisattva mahāsattva, abiding in the perfection of wisdom through the yoga of non-abiding, should fulfill the perfection of generosity through the yoga of non-renunciation."
Based on the non-apprehension of those who give, those who receive, and the gift itself,

the perfection of ethical discipline (*śīlapāramitā*) should be fulfilled by way of the non-existence of transgression, non-transgression, and the absence of committing a transgression; the perfection of patience (*kṣāntipāramitā*) should be fulfilled by way of imperturbability.
The perfection of vigor is to be fulfilled by means of the non-laxity of physical and mental vigor;
the perfection of meditation is to be fulfilled by means of the absence of intoxication, pride, and relish regarding meditation;
the perfection of wisdom is to be fulfilled by means of the non-apprehension of all phenomena.
Śāradvatīputra, a bodhisattva mahāsattva, abiding in the perfection of wisdom, should fulfill the four foundations of mindfulness by means of the non-apprehension of mindfulness.
Likewise [he should fulfill] the four right efforts,
the four bases of psychic power, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of enlightenment, and the noble eightfold path.

The concentration on emptiness (*śūnyatā-samādhi*) must be fulfilled; the signless concentration (*ānimitta-samādhi*) and the wishless concentration (*apraṇihita-samādhi*) must be fulfilled. The four meditative absorptions (*dhyāna*), the four immeasurables (*apramāṇa*), the four formless attainments (*ārūpya-samāpatti*), the eight liberations (*vimokṣa*), the nine successive attainments (*anupūrva-samāpatti*), the five superknowledges (*abhijñā*), and the nine perceptions—the perception of the nature of disease and so forth—must be fulfilled.
The perception of the festering, the perception of the putrid,
and the perception of the blood-stained.
The perception of the livid corpse; the perception of the devoured corpse; the perception of the scattered corpse.
The perception of a skeleton; the perception of a festering corpse;

mindfulness of the Buddha; mindfulness of the Dharma; mindfulness of the Saṅgha; mindfulness of ethical discipline; mindfulness of relinquishment; mindfulness of the deities; mindfulness of inhalation and exhalation; mindfulness of disenchantment; mindfulness of death; and mindfulness directed toward the body.
The perception of impermanence, the perception of suffering,
the perception of non-self,
the perception of impurity, the perception of death, and the perception of lack of delight in the entire world.
Throughout the world, there is the perception of distrust;

the knowledge of suffering, the knowledge of its origin, the knowledge of its cessation, the knowledge of the path, the knowledge of destruction, the knowledge of non-arising, the knowledge of phenomena (*dharmajñāna*), the subsequent knowledge (*anvayajñāna*), conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛtijñāna*), analytical knowledge (*paricayajñāna*), and knowledge as it truly is, accompanied by applied thought (*savitarka*).

Concentration with investigation (*savicāra*) but without applied thought (*avitarka*), concentration consisting of investigation alone (*vicāramātra*), and concentration without applied thought or investigation (*avitarka-avicāra*); the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown" (*anājñātamājñāsyāmītīndriya*), the faculty of knowing (*ājñendriya*), and the faculty of one who has known (*ājñātāvīndriya*); the bases of mastery (*abhibhvāyatana*), the bases of totality (*kṛtsnāyatana*), the four means of attraction (*saṃgrahavastu*), and the four systematic arrangements (*vyavasthāna*).
The ten stages, the ten practices, the ten patiences, the twenty resolute intentions, the knowledge of omniscience, the knowledge of tranquility and insight,
the three sciences, the four analytical knowledges, the four fearlessnesses, the five unshakable superknowledges, and the six...

One who desires to fully awaken to the seven perfections, the seven riches, the eight thoughts of a great person, the nine abodes of beings, the ten powers of a Tathāgata, the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha, great loving-kindness, great compassion, and the knowledge of omniscience endowed with the excellence of all modes, [should train in] the knowledge of the aspects of the path, omniscience, and the knowledge of the modes of the mental activities of all sentient beings.

A bodhisattva mahāsattva who wishes to bring [the perfections] to fulfillment should apply themselves to the perfection of wisdom; a bodhisattva mahāsattva who wishes to abandon all afflictions along with their latencies and habitual tendencies should apply themselves to the perfection of wisdom. It is in this way, Śāradvatīputra, that a bodhisattva mahāsattva should train in the perfection of wisdom.
Śāradvatīputra, a bodhisattva mahāsattva who wishes to enter the fixed course of a bodhisattva should train in the perfection of wisdom.

A bodhisattva mahāsattva who wishes to understand the stages of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, who wishes to transcend those stages, and who wishes to abide on the stage of non-retrogression, should train in the perfection of wisdom.

A bodhisattva mahāsattva who wishes to abide in the six superknowledges (*ṣaḍabhijñā*), who wishes to know the movements and fluctuations of the minds and conduct of all sentient beings, who wishes to surpass the knowledge of all śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, and who likewise wishes to attain the gateways of dhāraṇīs and the gateways of samādhis, should train in the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*).

If one wishes to surpass with a single thought-moment accompanied by sympathetic joy all that root of merit— from the giving of gifts up to the cultivation of wisdom— by all sons of good family and daughters of good family belonging to the vehicles of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, as well as the morality, concentration, wisdom, liberation, and the knowledge and vision of liberation of all those śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas; (LPG 9v)
A bodhisattva mahāsattva who wishes to surpass the meditations, liberations, concentrations, and attainments by means of a single thought-moment accompanied by sympathetic joy,
should train in the perfection of wisdom.
One should practice the yoga of the perfection of wisdom.

A bodhisattva mahāsattva should train in the perfection of wisdom so that even a small gift, through the application of dedication (*pariṇāmanā*), may become immeasurable, incalculable, infinite, and boundless. Likewise,
for one who maintains a small amount of ethical discipline, cultivates patience, exerts a small amount of vigor,

enters a small degree of meditative concentration, or cultivates a small amount of wisdom, [he should train] so that, through the application of dedication, it may become immeasurable, incalculable, infinite, and boundless.
Thinking, "May it be so," a bodhisattva mahāsattva should train in the perfection of wisdom.
Furthermore, Śāradvatīputra, a bodhisattva mahāsattva who wishes to abide in the perfection of generosity, who wishes to fulfill the perfection of generosity;
who wishes to practice the perfection of ethical discipline,
and who wishes to fulfill the perfection of ethical discipline—
by one who wishes to practice the perfection of patience,
by one who wishes to fulfill the perfection of patience,
and by one who wishes to practice the perfection of vigor;
One who desires to fulfill the perfection of vigor,
one who desires to practice the perfection of meditative concentration,
and one who desires to fulfill the perfection of meditative concentration, should practice the perfection of wisdom; one should train in the perfection of wisdom.
"If I would have the vision of the Buddha’s form in every birth,
and the exhortation of the Buddha; if I would have the Buddha’s mindfulness, the propitiation of the Buddha, and the acceptance by the Buddha," one should train in the perfection of wisdom.
Furthermore, Śāradvatīputra, a bodhisattva mahāsattva who wishes to bring the Buddha-body to perfection, who wishes to obtain the thirty-two marks of a great man,

who wishes to obtain the eighty secondary characteristics, and who wishes for the recollection of births in every lifetime and the non-forgetfulness of the thought of awakening, should train in the perfection of wisdom.
By one who desires to attain the state of never forgetting the conduct of all bodhisattvas;

by one who desires to avoid all evil friends and evil companions; by one who desires to please all Buddhas, bodhisattvas, and spiritual friends; by one who desires to conquer all Māras and the deities belonging to the host of Māra; [and] by one who desires [to overcome] all hindrances...
A bodhisattva mahāsattva who wishes to purify [all things] and who wishes to attain the state of non-obstruction regarding all phenomena should train in the perfection of wisdom.

A bodhisattva mahāsattva who wishes to bring the family of bodhisattvas to fulfillment, who wishes to please the family of Buddhas, and who wishes to remain so as not to interrupt the lineage of the Three Jewels, should train in the perfection of wisdom.

A bodhisattva mahāsattva who wishes to reach the stage of a youth, who wishes never to be separated from the Buddhas and bodhisattvas, who wishes to transcend the stages of a bodhisattva, and who wishes to swiftly fulfill the stage of a Tathāgata,
should train in the perfection of wisdom.

A bodhisattva mahāsattva should train in the perfection of wisdom with the thought: "May those roots of virtue and those modes by which I desire to honor, revere, respect, and worship the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, be successfully accomplished for me."
Desiring to satisfy all sentient beings, desiring to fulfill the hopes of all sentient beings—

with food, drink, vehicles, clothing, ornaments, flowers, garlands, perfumes, ointments, beds, seats, shelters, medicinal requisites for the sick, and all manner of utensils and enjoyments— for all sentient beings.
Thinking, "I shall fully satisfy [all beings]," a bodhisattva mahāsattva should apply himself to the perfection of wisdom.

Furthermore, Śāradvatīputra, a bodhisattva mahāsattva who wishes to establish all sentient beings— in as many world systems in the ten directions as there are grains of sand in the river Gaṅgā— in the ten paths of wholesome action; who wishes to establish them in the four meditative concentrations, the four immeasurables, the five superknowledges, and the taking of the three refuges and the attainment of serene confidence in the Buddha, Dharma, and Saṅgha, must [practice] the perfection of wisdom.
One should train [in this].
Or, by a bodhisattva mahāsattva who desires to encourage all those beings in world-systems as numerous as the sands of the river Gaṅgā toward the Mahāyāna,
and who desires to establish them in the perfection of giving, the perfection of ethical discipline, the perfection of patience, the perfection of vigor,
the perfection of meditative concentration, and the perfection of wisdom.
One should train in the perfection of wisdom.

Furthermore, Śāradvatīputra, a bodhisattva mahāsattva who wishes to make even a single arising of a wholesome thought inexhaustible until sitting at the seat of awakening should train in the perfection of wisdom.

Furthermore, Śāradvatīputra, those Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, who are in the world-systems of the eastern direction as numerous as the sands of the river Gaṅgā, and those Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, who are in the world-systems of the southern, western, northern, downward, upward, and indeed throughout all ten directions as numerous as the sands of the river Gaṅgā— they shall speak my praise.
Thus should a bodhisattva mahāsattva train in the perfection of wisdom.

Furthermore, Śāradvatīputra, a bodhisattva mahāsattva who wishes to approach, in a single production of thought, all those buddha-fields in the eastern direction that are as numerous as the sands of the river Gaṅgā, should train in the perfection of wisdom.

In this way, a bodhisattva mahāsattva who wishes to approach, with a single production of thought, all those buddha-fields as numerous as the sands of the river Gaṅgā— in the south, the west, the north, below, above, and indeed throughout the ten directions— should train in the perfection of wisdom.

Furthermore, Śāradvatīputra, a bodhisattva mahāsattva who wishes to make known as many buddha-fields in the eastern direction as there are grains of sand in the river Gaṅgā by means of a single sound-voice should train in the perfection of wisdom.

In the same way, a bodhisattva mahāsattva who wishes to make known as many Buddha-fields as there are grains of sand in the river Ganges— in the south, the west, the north, below, above, and indeed throughout all ten directions— should train in the perfection of wisdom.

Furthermore, Śāradvatīputra, a bodhisattva mahāsattva who wishes to remain so that the arising of Buddhas is not interrupted, who wishes to protect the family of bodhisattvas, and who wishes to remain so that the lineage of Buddhas is not severed, should train in the perfection of wisdom.
One who wishes to abide in internal emptiness, in external emptiness, in internal-and-external emptiness,
in the emptiness of emptiness,
and in great emptiness...
In the emptiness of the ultimate, in the emptiness of the conditioned, in the emptiness of the unconditioned, and in the emptiness of the absolute.
In the emptiness of that which is without beginning or end;
in the emptiness of non-dispersal;
in the emptiness of intrinsic nature.
In the emptiness of specific characteristics,
in the emptiness of all phenomena,
in the emptiness of non-apprehension, and in the emptiness of non-existence.
A bodhisattva mahāsattva who wishes to abide in the emptiness of intrinsic nature and the emptiness of the intrinsic nature of non-existence should train in the perfection of wisdom.
A bodhisattva mahāsattva who wishes to thoroughly understand the conditions of objective support, dominant influence, immediate antecedence, and causal efficiency,
and who wishes to realize the characteristics of their respective modes, should train in the perfection of wisdom.

A bodhisattva mahāsattva who wishes to realize the suchness of all phenomena— their non-falsity, their non-otherness, their unchanging suchness, and their suchness as it truly is— should train in the perfection of wisdom.

A bodhisattva mahāsattva who wishes to realize the dharma-realm of all phenomena, and who wishes to realize the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*) of all phenomena, should train in the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*).

Furthermore, Śāradvatīputra, a bodhisattva mahāsattva who wishes to know all the grains of sand in the Ganges River within as many trichiliocosm great thousandfold world-systems as there may be, should train in the perfection of wisdom.

A bodhisattva mahāsattva who wishes to lift up with the tip of a hair split a hundred times all the masses of water in the great oceans, rivers, great rivers, small streams, springs, lakes, ponds, and pools within the triple-thousand great-thousandfold world-system, and who does not wish to harm the living beings dependent upon them, [should train] in the perfection of wisdom.
One should train [in this].

Furthermore, Śāradvatīputra, if the entire mass of fire within the triple-thousand great-thousand world system were to become a single flame— as it does, for example, when the conflagration at the end of an aeon is occurring— a bodhisattva mahāsattva who wishes to extinguish it with a single breath from his mouth should train in the perfection of wisdom.

Furthermore, Śāradvatīputra, suppose there were whirlwinds in this trichiliocosm that could shake, scatter, and destroy this trichiliocosm, just as one might handle a handful of chaff; and suppose someone,
wishing to cover and restrain them all with the tip of a single finger, [were to attempt to do so].
A bodhisattva mahāsattva should train in the perfection of wisdom.

Furthermore, Śāradvatīputra, a bodhisattva mahāsattva who wishes to pervade the entire space-element within the triple-thousand great-thousand world-system with a single cross-legged posture should train in the perfection of wisdom.

Furthermore, Śāradvatīputra, a bodhisattva mahāsattva should train in the perfection of wisdom with the thought: "May I bind all the Sumerus, Cakravāḍas, and Mahācakravāḍas— the kings of mountains— within the triple-thousand great thousandfold world system with a single hair, lift them up, and cast them into immeasurable and incalculable world systems."

Furthermore, Śāradvatīputra, a bodhisattva mahāsattva who wishes to know, by means of the application of the analysis into atoms, all the grasses, trees, shrubs, herbs, and forest giants, as well as the heaps of clods of earth, sticks, pebbles, stones, mountains, and the great earth within the triple-thousand great-thousandfold world system, should train in the perfection of wisdom.

Furthermore, Śāradvatīputra, suppose one wishes to provide for all the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, together with their bodhisattvas and their assemblies of śrāvakas, in as many world systems in the eastern direction as there are grains of sand in the river Gaṅgā,
by means of a single alms-offering, a single flower, a single garland, a single fragrance, a single ointment, a single powder, a single robe, a single parasol, a single banner, and a single pennant.

A bodhisattva mahāsattva who wishes to honor, revere, respect, and worship all those Tathāgatas, Arhats, and perfectly enlightened Buddhas, together with the Bodhisattvas and the community of Śrāvakas, should train in the perfection of wisdom.

In the same way, in the southern direction, the western, the northern, below, above, and indeed all around in the ten directions— in each and every direction— one who wishes to provide for all the Buddhas, Blessed Ones, together with their bodhisattvas and their assemblies of śrāvakas, in world-systems as numerous as the sands of the river Gaṅgā, with a single alms-offering, a single flower, a single garland, a single fragrance, a single unguent, a single powder, a single robe, a single parasol, a single banner, and a single flag;

A bodhisattva mahāsattva who wishes to honor, revere, respect, and worship all those Tathāgatas, Arhats, and perfectly awakened Buddhas, together with the Bodhisattvas and the community of Śrāvakas, should train in the perfection of wisdom.

Furthermore, Śāradvatīputra, one who wishes to establish all those beings in the world-systems of the eastern direction—as numerous as the sands of the river Gaṅgā—in the aggregate of ethical discipline; likewise, wishing to establish them in the aggregate of concentration, the aggregate of wisdom, the aggregate of liberation, and the aggregate of the knowledge and vision of liberation; and likewise, wishing to establish them in the fruit of stream-entry.

A bodhisattva mahāsattva who wishes to establish others in the fruit of once-returning, the fruit of non-returning, arhatship, pratyekabuddhahood, and even in the realm of nirvana without remainder, should train in the perfection of wisdom.

In the same way, in the southern direction, in the western, in the northern, below, above, and indeed in all ten directions, one who wishes to establish all those beings in as many world-systems as there are grains of sand in the river Gaṅgā within the aggregate of ethical discipline, and likewise in the aggregate of meditative concentration and the aggregate of wisdom;

A bodhisattva mahāsattva who wishes to establish others in the aggregate of liberation and the aggregate of the knowledge and vision of liberation; who likewise wishes to establish them in the fruit of stream-entry, the fruit of once-returning, arhatship, pratyekabuddhahood, and even in the realm of nirvana without remainder— must train in the perfection of wisdom.

Furthermore, Śāradvatīputra, a bodhisattva mahāsattva who wishes to lead all sentient beings— however many there may be in all the world systems throughout the worlds of the ten directions— to final nirvāṇa by means of the vehicle of the śrāvakas and the vehicle of the pratyekabuddhas, must train in the perfection of wisdom.

Furthermore, Śāradvatīputra, a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom while giving a gift should train in this way: "By giving a gift in such a manner, it becomes of great fruit; by giving a gift in such a manner, one is reborn in the families of great kṣatriya clans."
In this way, one is reborn in families of great brahmins;
one is reborn in families of great householders;
and by giving such a gift, relying upon that very gift, one is reborn among the gods of the Realm of the Four Great Kings.

In this way, one is reborn among the gods of the Trāyastriṃśa, Yāma, Tuṣita, Nirmāṇarati, and Paranirmitavaśavartin realms. Having given such a gift, by relying on that very gift, one enters the first dhyāna; the second, third, and fourth dhyānas are produced; and one enters the attainment of the sphere of infinite space.

One enters the attainment of the sphere of infinite consciousness, the attainment of the sphere of nothingness, and the attainment of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception; having given a gift in this way, the noble eightfold path is produced,
and thus the fruit of stream-entry is attained,
and the fruit of once-returning is attained.
The fruit of non-returning is attained; arhatship is attained;
pratyekabuddhahood is attained; and unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment is attained.

Furthermore, Śāradvatīputra, a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing in the perfection of wisdom knows that by means of such skill in means, when giving a gift, he fulfills the perfection of generosity; in this way, he fulfills the perfection of ethical discipline, the perfection of patience, the perfection of vigor, the perfection of meditative concentration, and the perfection of wisdom.
Then the venerable Śāradvatīputra said this to the Blessed One: "Blessed One, how does a bodhisattva mahāsattva, while giving a gift, fulfill the perfection of generosity?"
"How is it that the perfection of wisdom becomes fulfilled?
The Blessed One said, "By way of non-apprehension, Śāradvatīputra."
Through the complete purity of the three spheres regarding the gift, the giver, and the recipient, the perfection of generosity is fulfilled.
Likewise, based on the state of neither transgression nor non-transgression, the perfection of ethical discipline is fulfilled;
and based on the state of being unshakeable, the perfection of patience is fulfilled.
The perfection of vigor consists in the non-slackening of physical and mental energy;
the perfection of meditation is based on non-distraction and the absence of conceptual construction;
and the perfection of wisdom is fulfilled through the yoga of non-apprehension while thoroughly understanding all phenomena.
Furthermore, Śāradvatīputra, a bodhisattva mahāsattva who wishes to know and to attain all the qualities of the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, of the past, future, and present,
should train in the perfection of wisdom.
Furthermore, Śāradvatīputra, a bodhisattva mahāsattva who wishes to go to the further shore of conditioned and unconditioned phenomena should train in the perfection of wisdom.

In this way, a bodhisattva mahāsattva who wishes to reach the further shore of all phenomena— whether with outflows or without outflows, wholesome or unwholesome, mundane or supramundane, material or immaterial, determinate or indeterminate, definite or indefinite, conducive to liberation or not conducive to liberation, partaking of decline or partaking of distinction, the phenomena of ordinary persons or the phenomena of the noble ones, the phenomena of those in training or those beyond training, and the phenomena of śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, or bodhisattvas— should train in the perfection of wisdom.

Furthermore, Śāradvatīputra, a bodhisattva mahāsattva who wishes to realize the suchness (*tathatā*) of all dharmas—past, future, and present—should train in the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*).
One who wishes to reach the limit of non-arising (*anutpādakoṭi*) of all dharmas and to penetrate the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*) should train in the perfection of wisdom.
Furthermore, Śāradvatīputra, a bodhisattva mahāsattva who wishes to be a precursor to all śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas should train in the perfection of wisdom.
Furthermore, Śāradvatīputra, a bodhisattva mahāsattva who wishes to be an attendant to the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, should train in the perfection of wisdom.
Furthermore, Śāradvatīputra, a bodhisattva mahāsattva who wishes to become part of the inner retinue of the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, should train in the perfection of wisdom.
Furthermore, Śāradvatīputra, a bodhisattva mahāsattva who wishes to possess a great retinue and to obtain a retinue of bodhisattvas should train in the perfection of wisdom.
Furthermore, Śāradvatīputra, a bodhisattva mahāsattva who wishes to purify the offerings of all donors should train in the perfection of wisdom.
Furthermore, Śāradvatīputra, a bodhisattva mahāsattva who wishes to have a mind that does not grasp at giving,

who wishes to separate himself from a mind of immorality, who wishes to abandon a mind of malice, and who wishes not to give rise to a mind of laziness or a mind of faulty wisdom, should train in the perfection of wisdom.

Furthermore, Śāradvatīputra, a bodhisattva mahāsattva who wishes to establish all sentient beings in the basis of meritorious action consisting of giving; and who wishes to establish them in the basis of meritorious action consisting of ethical discipline, consisting of cultivation, accompanied by service, and accompanied by all medicinal herbs, should train in the perfection of wisdom.

Furthermore, Śāradvatīputra, a bodhisattva mahāsattva who wishes to accomplish all aspects of the five eyes—the flesh eye, the divine eye, the wisdom eye, the dharma eye, and the buddha eye—should train in the perfection of wisdom. Furthermore, Śāradvatīputra, as for the Buddha Bhagavans in the worlds of the eastern direction, as numerous as the sands of the river Gaṅgā, and those in the southern direction... [and so forth].

Desiring to see with the divine eye all those Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, in as many world-systems as there are grains of sand in the river Ganges— in the west, the north, below, above, and indeed throughout the ten directions in every single direction—
and desiring to hear with the divine ear all the Dharma that those Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, proclaim;

A bodhisattva who desires to know with his own mind the minds of those Buddhas, the Blessed Ones; who desires to recollect the conduct of those Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, accompanied by their former lives;
and who desires to behold the manifold manifestations of the miraculous powers of those Buddhas, the Blessed Ones.
A great being should train in the perfection of wisdom.

Furthermore, Śāradvatīputra, a bodhisattva mahāsattva who hears the Dharma being taught by those Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, throughout the worlds in the ten directions as numerous as the sands of the river Gaṅgā, and who wishes to retain it through the application of the power of unbroken mindfulness until he has fully awakened to unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment— [should practice this concentration].
In this interval, one who wishes not to let anything go to waste should train in the perfection of wisdom.

Furthermore, Śāradvatīputra, a bodhisattva mahāsattva who wishes to bring to perfection the buddha-fields and the purifications of the buddha-fields of the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, of the past, future, and present, should train in the perfection of wisdom.

Furthermore, Śāradvatīputra, a bodhisattva mahāsattva who wishes to master all that has been spoken by the Tathāgata— whether it be discourses (*sūtra*), verses (*geya*), prophecies (*vyākaraṇa*), stanzas (*gāthā*), inspired utterances (*udāna*), introductory narratives (*nidāna*), parables (*ityuktaka*), birth stories (*jātaka*), extensive teachings (*vaipulya*), legends (*avadāna*), instructions (*upadeśa*), or marvelous events (*adbhutadharma*)— and which has not been heard by the disciples, must train in the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*).

Furthermore, Śāradvatīputra, whatever has been spoken, is being spoken, or will be spoken by all the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, in world-systems as numerous as the sands of the river Gaṅgā in the eastern direction— and likewise in the southern, western, northern, downward, upward, and indeed throughout the ten directions— whatever has been [spoken] by all the Buddhas:

A bodhisattva mahāsattva who wishes to hear, to take up, to retain, to master, and to proclaim in detail to others all that has been spoken, is being spoken, and will be spoken by the Blessed Ones, and who wishes to practice therein for the sake of suchness, should train in the perfection of wisdom.

Furthermore, Śāradvatīputra, it is because he desires to illuminate all those world-systems in the eastern direction— numerous as the sands of the river Gaṅgā— which are regions between worlds that are shrouded in darkness, thick with gloom, desolate, and filled with ruin, where even these two, the sun and the moon, though possessing such great supernatural power, such great majesty, and such great influence, do not shine, do not glow, and do not radiate light.
One should train in the perfection of wisdom.

In the same way, a bodhisattva mahāsattva who wishes to illuminate all those regions of blinding darkness in the southern direction, in the western, in the northern, below, above, and indeed throughout the ten directions in every respect, should train in the perfection of wisdom.

Furthermore, Śāradvatīputra, a bodhisattva who wishes to cause all sentient beings in as many world-systems in the eastern direction as there are grains of sand in the river Gaṅgā— world-systems where the sound of "Buddha" does not exist, nor the sound of "Dharma," nor the sound of "Saṃgha"— to hear those sounds of the Buddha, Dharma, and Saṃgha, and who wishes to establish them in right view; [should practice this perfection].
A mahāsattva should train in the perfection of wisdom.
In this same way, in the southern direction, in the western, in the northern, below, above, and so on, all around in the ten directions:

Furthermore, Śāradvatīputra, those sentient beings who are blind in the eastern direction, in the southern, western, northern, downward, upward, and indeed throughout the ten directions— in each direction as numerous as the sands of the river Gaṅgā— shall, through my power, see forms with their eyes; and those who are deaf shall hear sounds with their ears.
The insane shall hear [the teaching] and regain their mindfulness;
those who are naked shall obtain robes;
and those who are hungry and thirsty shall obtain food and drink.
The sick shall be completely freed from their diseases;
those who have fallen into bondage or imprisonment shall go wherever they desire by my supernatural power and my majesty.
That bodhisattva mahāsattva should train in the perfection of wisdom.

Why is this? It is so that those beings throughout the ten directions— in each direction, in world-systems as numerous as the sands of the river Ganges— who have fallen into the states of no-leisure or the miserable destinies, whether they be denizens of hell, animals, or inhabitants of the realm of Yama, may through my power pass away from there and obtain a human body.

A bodhisattva mahāsattva who wishes to establish all those sentient beings in ethical discipline; who wishes to establish them in meditative concentration, wisdom, liberation, and the knowledge and vision of liberation; and who wishes to establish them in the fruit of stream-entry, the fruit of once-returning, the fruit of non-returning, arhatship, pratyekabuddha-enlightenment, and even in unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
One should train in the perfection of wisdom.

Furthermore, Śāradvatīputra, a bodhisattva mahāsattva who wishes to train in the deportment of a Tathāgata, who wishes to train in the purity of the conduct and behavior of a Tathāgata, and who wishes to train in the purity of the bodily, vocal, and mental actions of a Tathāgata preceded by wisdom, should train in the perfection of wisdom.

Furthermore, Śāradvatīputra, a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom should investigate in this way: "How may I look with the gaze of an elephant? How may I yawn with the yawn of a great lion? How may I stride with the unfailing stride? How may I [leap] by a distance of four finger-breadths?"
May I travel without touching the great earth;

why should I not travel placing my two soles upon thousand-petaled lotuses, without harming the living beings dwelling beneath my feet? Why should I not travel adorning the great earth with the palms of my hands, which possess the design of thousand-spoked wheels?

"Why should I cause the great earth to revolve by the measure of a wheel all around? Why should I pace back and forth upon a walking-path? Why, as I am pacing across the entire great earth, should I not be smeared by the dust of the earth? Why [should I not traverse] one, two, three, or four yojanas?"
Whether five, ten, twenty, thirty, forty, or fifty yojanas;
or even up to a thousand yojanas,
or a hundred thousand yojanas.
Whether they be immeasurable, or incalculable, or inconceivable; or incomparable,
or infinite, or boundless.
One should train in the perfection of wisdom so that, while traveling through and wandering about immeasurable Buddha-fields, there is no fatigue of body nor weariness of mind.
"How might I, from beneath my two thousand-spoked wheels on the soles of my feet, emit hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of rays of light,
thereby pacifying all the sufferings of the unfortunate states and misfortunes, and bring all sentient beings to happiness"— thus should a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva train in the perfection of wisdom.
Furthermore, Śāradvatīputra, a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom should investigate in this way:

"How may I approach the seat of awakening surrounded and honored by many hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of gods, from those of the Four Great Kings up to those of the Akaniṣṭha heaven? Thus should one train in the perfection of wisdom.
Furthermore, Śāradvatīputra, a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom should investigate in this way:

"How may the gods of the Four Great Kings up to the Aghaniṣṭha gods prepare a spread of cloth for me as I sit at the foot of the Bodhi tree? In this manner, one should train in the perfection of wisdom. Furthermore, Śāradvatīputra, a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom should [investigate] in this way...
One should investigate thus: "How may that region of earth where I go, sit, or lie down after having fully awakened to unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment become composed of diamond?
For this reason, one should train in the perfection of wisdom.

Furthermore, Śāradvatīputra, a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom should investigate in this way: "How might I, on the very same day that I go forth, on that very same day realize unexcelled,
perfect, and complete awakening, and on that very same day set in motion the wheel of Dharma while setting it in motion?"
The dustless, stainless Dharma-eye regarding phenomena may be purified for immeasurable and incalculable beings;
the minds of immeasurable and incalculable beings may be liberated from the outflows through non-clinging; and immeasurable and incalculable beings may become irreversible.
If they would become [established] in unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, they should train in the perfection of wisdom.

Furthermore, Śāradvatīputra, a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom should generate this thought: "How may there be an immeasurable and incalculable community of śrāvakas for me when I have awakened to unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment; and how, through a single teaching of the Dharma, may there be immeasurable and incalculable arhats who attain realization while seated on a single seat?"

One should train in the perfection of wisdom with the thought: "May all bodhisattva mahāsattvas become irreversible from unexcelled, perfect, and complete awakening; may there be an immeasurable, incalculable, and infinite assembly of bodhisattvas; may my lifespan be immeasurable, and may my excellence of radiance be immeasurable. [One should train] so that I may attain unexcelled, perfect, and complete awakening.
One should train in the perfection of wisdom so that, once fully awakened in that buddha-field, even the word "attachment, aversion, and delusion" shall not exist.
"May all sentient beings be endowed with such wisdom as this: 'Excellent is giving; excellent is self-control; excellent is the holy life; excellent is non-violence toward all living beings.
May even the sound of the word 'disappearance of the True Dharma' not exist after I have attained parinirvāṇa. For this reason, that bodhisattva mahāsattva should train in the perfection of wisdom."
"How might sentient beings in world-systems as numerous as the sands of the river Gaṅgā become destined for unexcelled, perfect enlightenment merely by hearing my name?
For that reason, Śāradvatīputra, a bodhisattva mahāsattva should train in the perfection of wisdom.
Śāradvatīputra, at the time when a bodhisattva mahāsattva, practicing the perfection of wisdom, produces these qualities,
at that time the four great kings become joyful and think: "We shall here set down four alms-bowls, those which were set down by former great kings for former Tathāgatas."

The gods of the Heaven of the Thirty-three, the Yāmas, the Tuṣitas, and the Nirmāṇaratis become joyful; the gods who wield power over the creations of others also become joyful, thinking: "We shall perform service and attendance for him.
In this way, the hosts of Asuras will diminish, and the divine hosts will increase.
The gods of the Brahma-realm, the Ābhāsvara gods, the Śubhakṛtsna gods, the Bṛhatphala gods, the Avṛha gods, the Atapa gods,
the Sudṛśa gods, the Sudarśana gods, and the Aghaniṣṭha gods become joyful, thinking: "We shall entreat him to turn the wheel of Dharma."

Śāradvatīputra, at whatever time a bodhisattva mahāsattva, while coursing in the perfection of wisdom, increases in the six perfections, at that time sons of good family and daughters of good family become joyful in mind, thinking: "We shall become the mother and father of this mahāsattva."

"We shall become brothers, sisters, wives, sons, daughters, friends, ministers, kinsmen, and companions in joy. The Four Great Kings, up to the Aghaniṣṭha gods, become joyful because the Bodhisattva is established in the practice of non-sexual union;
he remains a celibate practitioner for the sake of establishing sentient beings in awakening, and is not bound by the qualities that lead to fettering.
He who is thus joined makes this vow:
"From the first production of the thought of enlightenment onward, I must be one who practices celibacy, not one who does not practice celibacy."
For what reason? Because for one who indulges in sensual desires, there is an obstacle to rebirth in the Brahma-world;
how much more so, then, is there an obstacle to unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment?
Therefore, a bodhisattva mahāsattva, having gone forth as one who practices celibacy, must realize unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment, and not as one who does not practice celibacy.

When this had been said, the venerable Śāradvatīputra addressed the Blessed One as follows: "Furthermore, must a bodhisattva mahāsattva necessarily have a wife, sons, and daughters? The Blessed One replied:
"Śāradvatīputra, for some bodhisattva mahāsattvas, there must necessarily be parents."
It is not necessarily the case that all [Bodhisattvas] have wives, sons, or daughters;
some Bodhisattva Mahāsattvas, Śāradvatīputra, from the moment of their first production of the thought of awakening, undertake the practice of celibacy (*brahmacarya*).
They remain eternally in the state of perpetual youth (*kumārabhūta*) until they fully awaken to unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment. Some [do so].

Furthermore, Śāradvatīputra, some bodhisattva mahāsattvas, through skill in means (*upāyakauśalya*), enjoy the five strands of sensual pleasure for the sake of maturing sentient beings and thereby awaken to unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment. Yet others, Śāradvatīputra, are bodhisattva mahāsattvas who have attained the profound perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*) and are free from the afflictions of desire; they [enjoy the enjoyment of the strands of sensual pleasure] for the sake of maturing sentient beings.
They produce [them], yet they do not consume them.
It is just as if, Śāradvatīputra, a skilled illusionist or an illusionist’s apprentice, well-trained in the knowledge of the application of the arts of illusion,

were to manifest the five strands of sensual pleasure and display himself as enjoying, playing, and diverting himself with those five strands of sensual pleasure. What do you think, Śāradvatīputra, would that illusionist or illusionist’s apprentice [be bound by them]?
"Or would the five qualities of sensual desire be experienced?
He replied, "Certainly not, Blessed One.

The Blessed One said, "In the very same way, Śāradvatīputra, bodhisattva mahāsattvas who are well-trained in the illusion of the Mahāyāna and have attained the dwelling in the illusory nature of phenomena [do not experience them]."
Free from all afflictions, yet by the power of great compassion for the sake of maturing beings to be trained, they display the enjoyment of the qualities of sensual pleasure;

yet they do not partake of those sensual pleasures, nor do they dwell together with them, nor are they defiled by them. In this manner, Śāradvatīputra, Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas speak in dispraise of sensual pleasures.
"Sensual pleasures are ablaze; sensual pleasures are loathsome; sensual pleasures are murderers; sensual pleasures are adversaries; sensual pleasures are enemies.

For in this way, Śāradvatīputra, bodhisattva mahāsattvas demonstrate the five strands of sensual pleasure for the sake of separating sentient beings from them and for the sake of dispassion toward them."
And they do not become intoxicated by them, nor do they become negligent; for the sake of sensual pleasures, nor on account of sensual pleasures, they do not commit sinful actions.

When this had been said, the venerable Śāradvatīputra addressed the Blessed One as follows: "But how, Blessed One, should a bodhisattva mahāsattva course in the perfection of wisdom? The Blessed One replied:
"In this regard, Śāradvatīputra, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva courses in the perfection of wisdom, he does not perceive 'a bodhisattva'."
He does not perceive even the name "bodhisattva";
he does not perceive even the conduct of a bodhisattva;
he does not perceive even "perfection of wisdom."
One does not perceive even the name "perfection of wisdom";
one does not perceive that "one practices," nor does one perceive that "one does not practice."
He does not perceive form, nor does he perceive feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness.
Why is that? Because that bodhisattva is empty by way of the intrinsic nature of name; it is not by way of emptiness that form is empty.
Neither feeling, perception, nor mental formations [are empty] by means of emptiness; consciousness is not empty by means of emptiness. Emptiness is not other than form;
emptiness is not other than feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness.
Form is itself emptiness; feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are themselves emptiness. Of what, then, [is it empty]?
For this reason: it is merely a name that this is called "awakening"; it is merely a name that this is called a "bodhisattva";
it is merely a name that this is called "emptiness";
it is merely a name that this is form, feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness.
For form is like an illusion; feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are like an illusion. An illusion is a mere name, neither located in a place nor located in a region.

It is non-existent, unreal, and equal to what is false—the appearance of an illusion. Being devoid of intrinsic nature, it is without intrinsic nature, unarisen, and unceasing; there is no decrease and no increase, no defilement and no purification. Practicing in this way, the bodhisattva mahāsattva does not perceive arising.
He does not perceive cessation;
he does not perceive a state;
he does not perceive decline.
He does not perceive increase;
he does not perceive affliction;
he does not perceive purification.
He does not perceive form;
he does not perceive feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness.
Even that which is called "awakening" or "bodhisattva," he does not perceive that either.

For what reason? Because these are artificial names; they are designated for each respective phenomenon by means of adventitious, unreal, and conceptually constructed designations used in conventional discourse.
And they become attached through conventional usage.
Therefore, a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing in the perfection of wisdom does not perceive any phenomena; not perceiving them, he does not conceive of them, nor does he become attached to them.
